extracted.intended_audience: classical philologists, translators, and textual critics working on Aristotle and ancient Greek texts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative standards for interpreting, translating, and restoring Aristotle's Poetics (and closely related esoteric works), including principles for textual criticism, manuscript evaluation, sense-selection, and emendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No interpretation is certain without chapter-and-verse citation
rubrics_metrics.description: No interpretation is certain for which chapter and verse cannot be cited from Aristotle’s works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require direct textual citation from Aristotle's corpus to support an interpretation; interpretations must be anchored in the author's own writings rather than conjecture or analogies alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for every syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: No interpretation is satisfactory which fails to account for every syllable of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory reading must explain all words (and apparent anomalies) in the clause or line; do not ignore or discard 'difficult' words without attempting to reconcile them with context, parallel usages, or manuscript evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ascribing unmeaning or commonsense-conflicting propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: No interpretation is tolerable which ascribes to Aristotle propositions which are unmeaning or which conflict with common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject emendations or readings that would make the author assert nonsense or clear contradictions with ordinary reasoning; prefer readings that preserve intelligibility and plausibility in light of Aristotle's known doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate aim of textual criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate aim of textual criticism is to restore the work of an author to the condition in which it left his hands; provisionally, one may aim to restore the text as it existed at some particular epoch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct restoration to the author's autograph is impossible, explicitly state and justify the intermediate stage being targeted (e.g., an archetype or medieval recension) before attempting deeper emendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore intermediate archetype when archetype postdates autograph
rubrics_metrics.description: If all existing copies are traceable to an archetype which was later than the author’s own copy, the text of that intermediate stage must be restored before attempting to reconstruct anything more original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish and restore the archetypal transmission stage (the common ancestor of extant MSS) as a necessary preliminary step; do not leap from corrupted copies directly to an imagined autograph without addressing the intermediate archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of convincing evidence for MSS relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Convincing internal evidence would be the occurrence in all MSS of defects traceable to a particular source; convincing external evidence would be reliable testimony linking MSS to that source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of common ancestry using both internal (shared errors, omissions, characteristic corruptions) and external (documentary statements, provenance, dated copies) evidence; require one or both kinds to be compelling before asserting direct derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer independent corroboration; be wary of 'easier' readings and deliberate emendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a manuscript offers an easier or more regular text, this is not by itself a reason to prefer it; some MSS show signs of deliberate emendation. The Arabic version and independent witnesses can guard against misleading readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer readings supported by multiple independent witnesses (including reliable translations like the Arabic or Syriac where applicable). Treat unexpectedly easy or smooth readings with suspicion as potential later editorial emendations; weigh palaeographic and historical plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use author's broader corpus and analogical rules to fix sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine word-sense and technical meaning by comparing usage across Aristotle's works (e.g., words with triadic senses such as 'measure'/'metre'/'extent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a term has multiple possible senses, consult parallel passages in Aristotle (and his systematic usages in works like Physics, Metaphysics, Ethics, Rhetoric) and apply analogical rules rather than forcing a single isolated gloss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret passages in light of whole work and cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of the Poetics (e.g., §4) are not intelligible without reference to later or other sections (§6, §26); understanding requires acquaintance with the whole treatise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and interpret passages in the context of the entire treatise and its cross-references; identify which questions are left open by earlier sections and which are settled later, rather than treating isolated passages as self-sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not introduce unwarranted supplements in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a formula or construction (e.g., etze—eite) implies supplemental apodoses in general usage, those supplements must not be inserted unless the sentence at hand admits them; sometimes the whole sentence must be retranslated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding implied phrases ('I know not', 'equally', etc.) not justified by the immediate Greek; if common supplemental readings do not fit the specific sentence, render it afresh without forcing familiar supplements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate metaphor from confusion when species stands for genus
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specific term seems used for a genus (species-for-genus), decide whether this is due to confusion or conscious metaphor according to the author's theory and consistent usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the author's doctrine (e.g., Aristotle's accounts of metaphor and naming) and look for internal consistency: if the usage fits an established metaphorical pattern, accept it; if not, examine whether confusion or accidental convention better explains the choice of species-term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and account for interpolations and historical tampering
rubrics_metrics.description: Some MSS and versions (Greek and Arabic) show Christian interpolation and other corruptions; such interpolations must be identified and treated as possible later additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert for anachronistic content, doctrinally motivated insertions, or stylistic departures from Aristotle; corroborate suspect passages against other recensions and versions, and explain why an interpolation is likely before excising or emending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess grammatical oddities against author's idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: A clumsy grammatical construction (e.g., combination of two participles, odd personification) need not be a solecism if it is consistent with the author's style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before postulating corruption or emendation for awkward grammar, check comparable constructions in the author's oeuvre and in later classical usage; accept awkward but authorial turns if they align with known idiom.
